cells.tense: Your hands are deciding right now what gets tended and what gets set down.
cells.act: do the giving in the open this time, where it was always done unseen
cells.ask: This week, do one caring thing where the person it's for can watch you do it. Set the table while they're there, or say the thing out loud instead of quietly covering it. One occasion is enough.
cells.core:
Something is arriving, and you're already meeting it well. Competing things stay alive at once, and the care isn't force — it's attention moving from one to the next in order, nothing dropped. That's the whole skill, and it's running.

One part of it stays out of sight. What needs doing gets done while backs are turned: gaps filled before anyone noticed them, needs met before they were spoken. It lands, and mostly it registers as nothing in particular — the household just holds. Pick one occasion this week and do the caring where it can be watched. Not announced. Just not hidden. When the hand is seen, the receiving goes easier, and so does the next round. Nothing about your timing has to change for that to be true.
cells.sheetLine: You already tend it well. Let some of it be seen.
cells.verb: deciding what to tend, with care, before it arrives
cells.place: at the threshold where what's coming enters

cells.tense: Tomorrow's demands are already laid out and you're setting places for all of them tonight.
cells.act: walk through the thing you built and touch nothing
cells.ask: Walk through something you've already tended — the setup, the arrangement — and adjust none of it. Look, touch nothing, fix nothing, schedule nothing. Then go do something else entirely.
cells.core:
Something's arriving and you're at the door with a plan for it. Two demands, three, all being arranged before they've landed — the next thing organised while this one is still coming through. The attention is real; it's simply running ahead of what's here, and the room keeps filling.

There's a version of this where the work rests. One way in: go through what you already made — the setup, the arrangement, the thing that works — and leave every part of it alone. No fixing, no improving, nothing shifted by a millimetre. Finished stays finished. If the urge to adjust something comes, that's fine, it can stay unscheduled. What feels satisfying has somewhere to land when nothing gets added on top of it.

cells.tense: The threshold has been crossed already, though your hands stayed at the last door.
cells.act: keep following the star after everything that has happened
cells.ask: Keep going toward the one you'd still choose if nothing shifted for a month. Ten minutes a week, four weeks, whether or not anything comes of it. No progress to report to anyone.
cells.core:
Something is coming in, and it isn't landing. What used to run without effort — the hands knowing what to do, the next thing already in view — isn't doing that now. Care is still there. It has nowhere to go, so it sits, and what's arriving waits.

Here's something that doesn't ask much: keep showing up for the one you'd still choose if nothing improved for a month. Ten minutes a week on the same thing, whether or not anything comes of it. No progress to report, nobody to tell. The point isn't to feel better about it. It's that the picking stays yours while nothing else is moving. The hands remember the way back before the heart does, and it doesn't have to shine first.
cells.sheetLine: You still care. Set ten minutes a week on the one you'd choose.

cells.tense: At the doorway you steady everything that comes through, and by your own account you're doing nothing.
cells.act: accept the acknowledgment when it comes
cells.ask: When someone thanks you for tending something, take it. Say you're glad it helped, then stop. Don't wave it off, don't credit someone else, don't explain that it was nothing.
cells.core:
Something's arriving and here you are at the door — steadying what comes through, keeping both demands alive at once. Other people notice. They call it the household running well, the team holding together, and you let the description stand. The deciding is happening. Your name isn't on it.

The next time someone thanks you for something you tended, don't hand it back. Take it, say you're glad it helped, stop there. No waving it off, no crediting someone else, no explaining how small it was. That's the whole act — a sentence accepted and held for two seconds. If it doesn't come this week, that's not a failure; you're allowed to let one land when it does. What you keep steady at the door is yours to have seen.
